result:
I've checked your claim against Anthropic's engineering posts and Google Research's summary of an agent-scaling study, and saved a note about it. Next is your answer.

More agents don't always give better results, so don't pick five or ten yet. **Start with one agent** that has tools for your manuals, calendar and bookings.

Take "If I'm trained on the laser cutter, book it for 3 pm." The assistant has to check your training and the open slot before it books. Splitting these dependent steps across agents (a **multi-agent system**) adds handoffs where information can get lost.

Extra agents can help when a big job splits into independent parts, such as researching several separate topics at once. In [Google Research's tests](https://research.google/blog/towards-a-science-of-scaling-agent-systems-when-and-why-agent-systems-work/) of 180 setups, a coordinated team scored about 81% higher than one agent on a finance task that could be split up. On a step-by-step planning task, every multi-agent version did 39–70% worse.

Cost matters for your budget. Models count text in **tokens** (small chunks of text), and more tokens generally cost more. [Anthropic reports](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system) that in its data, agents typically used about 4 times the tokens of a chat, and multi-agent systems about 15 times. These figures don't predict your costs or compare five agents with ten.

For your design review, you could say: "We'll start with one agent, test it on real student requests, and add complexity only if tests show a gain worth the cost." This follows [Anthropic's advice on building agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents), a good next read.

**Quick check:** which is easier to split between agents, and why?
- A. Summarizing the safety rules in three unrelated machine manuals
- B. Finding a student's free time, then booking a machine for that time

I can turn this into a short lesson if you'd like. It would also help to cover tokens and context first, since they affect this choice.
